This research delves into the difficulties associated with using physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to solve complex, high-dimensional ordinary differential equations (ODEs) that arise in real-world applications. We examine the limitations of this approach through a series of numerical experiments, highlighting how PINN models can fail to capture solutions to certain high-dimensional ODEs, even when using sufficient training data. Our findings indicate that the emergence of "rogue modes" within the neural network is a key factor contributing to these failures, and we develop a theoretical framework to explain this phenomenon. We also identify a specific condition that determines whether the PINN model will be able to learn the solution to the ODE, and provide a method for detecting when this approach is likely to fail in advance. Our results demonstrate that the efficacy of PINN models in solving high-dimensional ODEs is heavily dependent on the specific problem at hand, and we offer guidance on how to approach these challenges effectively. The accompanying code for these experiments is available on GitHub at https://github.com/berkeley-statistics/rogue-mode-pinn. Current video conferencing applications employ pre-encoded videos, but these are often severely degraded under adverse network conditions, leading to poor viewing experiences. Moreover, the use of existing video codecs under these conditions is inadequate, resulting in subpar video quality. This paper addresses this issue by introducing a novel approach to dynamically adjust and improve video quality in real-time, even in low-bitrate scenarios. By leveraging a pre-trained video encoder, a video quality assessment module, and a quality-based adaptive policy, our method can identify and enhance low-quality regions within videos, even in the absence of complete image information. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed technique can significantly enhance the visual quality of pre-encoded videos, resulting in noticeable improvements in subjective video quality and a substantial reduction in packet transmission rates. This innovation has the potential to revolutionize video conferencing applications by providing a seamless and high-quality viewing experience, even in the face of limited network resources. This research presents a novel method for categorizing documents in open access archives based on their internal file content. We evaluated this approach by applying it to the entire collection of documents from the Swedish CIVILICA repository, containing 135,869 thesis and conference papers, of which 36% lacked relevant metadata. Utilizing a supervised machine learning model, we successfully classified the majority of these documents, achieving an accuracy rate of 92%. The findings suggest that internal file metadata can be a valuable resource for document categorization, particularly in cases where metadata is incomplete or unavailable. Furthermore, this approach may be adapted for application in other large-scale document repositories. The accompanying source code is available in a public GitHub repository. Additionally, the dataset used in this research has been uploaded to Zenodo. Access to the research report is provided through the DiVA digital library. The methodology and code can be accessed via GitHub. The dataset used in this research is available on Zenodo. Finally, we outline potential future research directions that build upon this study.

This paper presents a novel approach to this problem, where we utilize a deep learning model to create a probabilistic map of uncertainty, and then employ a method that focuses on reinforcing existing beliefs rather than simply identifying areas of uncertainty. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in comparison to existing approaches, and also show that it can be used to improve the performance of downstream tasks in autonomous vehicles by leveraging a method of informed data sampling. Experimental results validate the superiority of our method compared to current state-of-the-art methods for uncertainty mapping and show that it can also improve the performance of downstream tasks in a more efficient manner.
